Landlord-Ready Checklist for Renters Before Moving Out

If you're renting, wall damage on departure day can cost you a significant chunk of your deposit — and it's entirely avoidable. I've helped several tenants prepare for move-out inspections, and having a clear checklist makes the whole thing far less stressful.

Landlords are looking for damage beyond fair wear and tear. A nail hole is fair wear and tear; a ripped patch of plaster or a greasy adhesive stain is not.

Pre-Move-Out Wall Check — Room by Room

  • Walk every room and photograph all four walls before you start cleaning — date-stamped photos are your best evidence
  • Fill all nail holes and small damage with appropriate filler and sand smooth
  • Touch up paint on any filled areas — feather the edges and use a mini roller for the closest texture match
  • Remove all adhesive residue from walls, skirting boards and door frames
  • Check picture rail hooks are removed and the rail is undamaged
  • Inspect wall surfaces in raking light (a torch held at a low angle to the wall works brilliantly) — this shows up dents and surface damage that looks invisible in normal light
  • Re-photograph all repaired areas once complete — after and before shots together are ideal
  • Check window frames, skirting, and door surround areas where adhesive strips may have been used
  • Return any landlord-supplied fixings (curtain rails, shelving brackets) to their original positions if you moved them
  • Keep receipts for any filler, paint, or repair materials — some landlords will accept proof of good-faith repairs in lieu of deductions
Pro Tip: Do your wall repairs at least 48 hours before the check-out inspection — freshly painted patches are obvious and actually draw attention. Give everything time to dry, cure, and settle so the finish looks natural rather than rushed.

How to Avoid Damage Next Time with Renter-Friendly Hanging Solutions

Now that everything is down and your walls are looking good, let's talk about how to hang things the right way next time — so this whole process is much easier when it comes around again. Because let's be honest, you're going to want to put something back up. A bare wall is not a happy wall.

The renter-friendly hanging world has come on enormously in the past few years. There are genuinely good options now that look beautiful, hold real weight, and come down without drama.

Best Renter-Friendly Hanging Solutions

  • Command strips (weight-rated): The classic option — make sure you choose the correct weight rating for your piece and always follow the preparation steps (clean wall, press firmly for 30 seconds, wait one hour before loading). They really do work when used correctly.
  • Picture rails with adjustable cords: If your property has picture rails (common in older UK homes), use them — they're the single best renter-friendly system available. No holes, complete flexibility, and entirely reversible.
  • Adhesive picture hanging strips with velcro-style interlocking: Ideal for lighter frames. The two-part system means you can remove the frame without disturbing the wall adhesive.
  • Washi tape or decorative tape for paper art and prints: For lightweight prints on card or paper, washi tape on the back of a mount is genuinely damage-free and adds a decorative touch to the display itself.
  • Freestanding frames and easels: An underrated option for large statement pieces — no wall contact at all, fully flexible positioning, and gorgeous in the right space.
  • Floating shelf ledges on Command-strip brackets: Allows you to prop and lean art rather than fixing it directly — incredibly versatile and completely renter-safe.

One of my favourite clients — a young woman in a rented flat in Edinburgh — had a strict no-nails clause in her tenancy. We styled her whole living room using picture rail hooks, two floating ledges on adhesive brackets, and a freestanding floor-leaning mirror. It looked incredible, completely unlocked the space, and she moved out with her full deposit intact. The right system genuinely makes all the difference.

Pro Tip: Always check your tenancy agreement before hanging anything — some landlords specify the exact types of fixings allowed, and using anything else (even Command strips) can technically be a breach. A quick message to your landlord in writing is the safest approach and creates a useful paper trail.

Product Recommendations Worth Knowing About

I'm not here to push products at you for the sake of it — but some genuinely make the whole removal and rehanging process dramatically easier, and I want to flag the categories worth looking for.

These are the product types I reach for and recommend to clients regularly, based on what actually works rather than what's simply popular.

Recommended Product Categories

  • Citrus-based adhesive remover (e.g., Goo Gone): Safe on most painted walls, effective on greasy adhesive residue, and doesn't strip paint if used carefully with the instructions followed
  • Spackle pens: The easiest possible way to fill small nail holes — no mixing, no mess, and the fine tip gives precision you can't get from a traditional filler knife on a small hole
  • Command strip removal tool: The official plastic tool designed specifically to help stretch and release Command strip tabs — dramatically reduces the risk of strip breakage mid-release
  • Fine-finish pre-mixed filler: For anything bigger than a pin hole — a lightweight pre-mixed formula sands to a beautifully smooth surface that regular polyfilla simply can't match
  • Tester pots of wall paint: Keep one from your original paint job or get one colour-matched — a tester pot is the perfect size for touch-up work and far more economical than a full tin
  • Picture hanging strips (velcro-style, weight-rated): The alternative to Command strips — the two-part system means you can remove the art without disturbing the wall adhesive
  • Dental floss (plain, unwaxed): Genuinely one of the most effective free tools for sliding behind adhesive-mounted items — buy a spare pack and keep it in your toolkit permanently
Pro Tip: Always read the label before applying any adhesive remover to your specific wall finish — citrus-based removers are generally safe on standard emulsion paint but some specialist finishes (chalk paint, limewash, textured coatings) can react differently. A small test patch in a hidden corner takes two minutes and could save you a significant repair job.

Damage-free removal isn't just about being careful — it's about being informed. Whether you're a renter preparing for a move, a homeowner doing a seasonal refresh, or someone who simply made a hanging decision they now regret — there's a clean, careful solution for every situation on every surface.

The best way to layer textures in a boho style is to start with a neutral base, then build up in stages — rough naturals first, soft fabrics second, and decorative accents last — so every element earns its place without the room feeling cluttered or chaotic. These boho texture layering ideas work across every room and every budget, and I'm going to walk you through exactly how to do it.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in a room that felt genuinely warm and interesting — full of personality, all those gorgeous layers of fabric and natural material — and thought, "How on earth did they do that without it looking a mess?" I get asked this all the time, and it's exactly the kind of question I love answering, especially when it comes to wall art and the textural story it tells in a boho home.

Quick answer: Layer boho textures by starting with a neutral wall and floor, then adding rough naturals like jute and rattan, followed by soft layers such as woven throws and cushions, and finally decorative accents like macramé, plants, and wall art. Work room by room, keep your colour palette cohesive, and always step back to edit — less is almost always more than you think.

Boho style is one of the most misunderstood looks in home decor. It's not about piling everything you love onto every surface and hoping for the best. True boho layering is a considered process — a way of combining natural materials, handmade touches, global-inspired patterns, and unique wall art to create rooms that feel curated, not cluttered. When you add in the right unique home decor pieces, the whole thing clicks into place in a way that feels genuinely personal and lived-in.

Start with a Neutral Base for Boho Texture Layering

Before you add a single cushion or a woven wall hanging, you need a calm, neutral backdrop that lets your layers breathe. Think warm whites, soft creams, sandy beiges, and warm greiges — these give every subsequent layer somewhere to land without competing with it.

Your walls, your main flooring, and your largest furniture pieces should all sit in this neutral zone. If your sofa is already a bold colour or pattern, that's fine — just treat it as one of your mid layers rather than your base.

How to Build a Neutral Base

  • Walls: Choose warm white, linen, or soft clay. Avoid cool greys — they fight boho's earthy warmth.
  • Flooring: Natural wood, stone tile, or concrete are ideal. If you have carpet, a large flat-weave rug on top will anchor the base layer.
  • Large furniture: Stick to undyed linen, canvas, or cotton in oatmeal, cream, or warm taupe tones.
  • Ceiling: Keep it white or very pale. A warm-toned ceiling instantly lifts a room without adding visual noise.
  • Window treatments: Linen or cotton curtains in a natural, unbleached shade work perfectly as part of the base.

I once helped a client who'd painted her living room a lovely deep terracotta and then couldn't work out why all her boho layers looked too busy. The problem was there was no neutral breathing space — every single element was competing. We didn't repaint; instead, we pulled in much larger amounts of cream through a new rug and fresh linen throws, and it completely transformed the room.

Pro Tip: If you're renting and can't paint, use large-scale neutral textiles — a big cream linen throw draped over a sofa, sheer natural curtains, and a pale jute rug — to visually reset the base of the room without touching the walls.

Mix and Match Textures: Materials, Fabrics, and Finishes

Boho texture layering is all about contrast — rough against smooth, matte against sheen, natural against woven. The more genuinely different your materials feel to the touch, the more interesting the finished room looks to the eye.

The key rule I always come back to is this: never put two very similar textures next to each other. A jute rug next to a sisal basket works because the weave patterns are different enough. A jute rug next to a sisal cushion can look muddy and flat.

Boho Texture Material Pairings That Work

  • Jute + velvet: The ultimate boho contrast — rough and smooth in the same earthy colour family.
  • Rattan + linen: Rattan's geometric weave sits beautifully next to the soft drape of natural linen.
  • Ceramic + macramé: Hard, matte ceramics and soft, knotted cotton create real visual tension in a good way.
  • Sheepskin + woven cotton: Two soft textures that work because one is fluffy and dimensional, the other flat and structured.
  • Raw wood + silk-feel cushion covers: The roughness of undressed timber makes a lustrous fabric look even richer beside it.
  • Hammered brass + rough plaster wall: Metallic and matte create a striking but grounded combination.

Step-by-Step Boho Texture Layering Method for Walls and Decor

Layering textures isn't random — there's a real method to it, and once you understand it, you can apply it to any room. I think of it as working in four distinct passes, each one adding more specificity and personality than the last.

Don't try to do everything at once. Buy a piece, live with it for a few days, then add the next. Rushing is the single biggest reason boho rooms end up looking overwhelming rather than effortless.

The Four-Pass Method

  • Pass 1 — Neutral base: Walls, floor, and large furniture in calm neutrals (as covered above). This pass is mostly structural.
  • Pass 2 — Natural roughs: Add jute or sisal rugs, rattan furniture or accessories, wicker baskets, raw wooden shelves, terracotta pots. These ground the room with natural, earthy weight.
  • Pass 3 — Soft fabrics: Layer in throws, cushions, poufs, and curtains. Mix at least three different fabric textures — for example, a velvet cushion, a woven cotton throw, and a sheepskin.
  • Pass 4 — Decorative accents: This is where wall art, plants, candles, books, and small ceramics come in. These are the details that make the room feel personal and finished.

Here's what happened when I tried the four-pass method in my own flat's spare room: I kept buying Pass 4 items first — little pots, wall hangings, candles — and the room never came together. The moment I stripped it back and actually started with Pass 1, everything else found its place naturally. It felt like cheating, it was so much easier.

Pro Tip: After each pass, take a photo of the room on your phone. It's much easier to spot what's working and what's fighting for attention in a photo than it is standing in the space yourself.

Boho Wall Art as a Texture Layer: Prints, Tapestries, and Mixed Media

Wall art isn't just decoration in a boho room — it's a genuine texture layer in its own right. A woven tapestry adds the same kind of visual weight as a rug. A macramé wall hanging introduces knotted depth to a flat wall. Even a print in the right frame adds a matte-meets-glossy textural moment.

The mistake most people make is treating wall art as an afterthought — something to fill empty space once the room is "done." In boho layering, the wall is part of the texture story from the very beginning.

  • Woven tapestries: The original boho wall layer — handwoven pieces in natural fibres add warmth, pattern, and genuine three-dimensional texture.
  • Macramé wall hangings: Knotted cotton or jute with fringe; they cast soft shadows and add a sculptural quality to flat walls.

  • Mixed-media art: Pieces that incorporate fabrics, beads, or natural materials within the artwork itself add real physical depth.

  • Gallery walls with varied frame finishes: Mixing raw wood, rattan-wrapped, and thin black frames creates textural variety even before you look at what's inside the frames.

Bedroom Texture Layering

  • Start with natural linen or cotton bedding in cream or warm white — this is your base.
  • Layer a chunky knit or woven throw across the foot of the bed for tactile depth.
  • Add cushions in at least three different textures: velvet, woven cotton, and a bead-embroidered or embroidered cushion.
  • Hang a large macramé or woven textile above the bed instead of a headboard, or above a traditional headboard for extra texture height.
  • Use rattan or wicker beside tables, a sheepskin on the floor beside the bed, and trailing plants to bring the layering all the way to floor level.

Living Room Texture Layering

  • Ground the room with a large jute or flat-weave rug — size up; too-small rugs make layering look disjointed.
  • Layer a second, smaller patterned rug on top for a collected, well-travelled feel.
  • Mix sofa cushions across at least four textures: woven, velvet, embroidered, and tasselled.
  • Bring rattan, wicker, or woven baskets in as storage that also works as decor.
  • Use plants at different heights — a tall floor plant, a mid-height shelf plant, and trailing plants at high level to soften vertical space.

Entryway Texture Layering

  • A natural coir or jute doormat with a printed pattern introduces texture from the first step inside.
  • Add a small rattan console or wooden bench as the structural anchor.
  • Hang a macramé wall piece, a small mirror with a rattan or wooden frame, or a cluster of dried botanical wreaths on the wall.
  • A tall wicker basket for umbrellas or throws adds practical texture at floor level.
  • Layer a ceramic pot with a plant — trailing or compact — to soften the corner and bring life to the space immediately.

Colour Palette Guidance for Cohesive Boho Layered Looks

The single biggest thing that separates a boho room that looks professionally styled from one that just looks chaotic is a disciplined colour palette. Boho doesn't mean every colour at once — it means deep, earthy tones used with intention.

I always work to what I call a 3-1-1 palette: three neutral tones, one warm earth accent, and one deeper or contrasting pop. Everything in the room maps back to these five tones, no matter how varied the textures are.

Boho Colour Palette Rules

  • Neutrals (the majority): Warm white, cream, sand, linen, oatmeal — these should make up at least 60% of the room's visual colour.
  • Earth accent (the personality): Rust, terracotta, warm ochre, amber, or burnt sienna — introduce this through cushions, pots, throws, and wall art.
  • Deep pop (the drama): Deep teal, indigo, forest green, or aubergine — just one or two pieces in this tone to stop the room feeling too one-note.
  • Metallic (the finish): Warm brass or antique gold accents read as neutral in a boho palette but add a subtle luminosity that lifts natural materials.
  • What to avoid: Cool greys, bright white, neon tones, and pastel pinks — all of these fight the warm, earthy heart of boho style.

DIY Projects with Big Textural Impact

  • Basic macramé wall hanging: A wooden dowel and natural cotton cord are all you need. Square knots and half-hitch knots are beginner-level and create beautiful results. Fringe the ends for extra texture.
  • Dip-dyed fabric wall panel: Take a length of unbleached cotton canvas and dip the bottom third into fabric dye in a rust or indigo tone. Hang from a dowel when dry — it reads as abstract art with genuine textile texture.
  • Woven branch mobile: Collect interesting branches from outdoors, tie them together with jute twine, and hang small bundles of dried flowers, feathers, or beads from the lower branches. This is a genuine three-dimensional texture layer for the ceiling or a corner.
  • Yarn-wrapped pot cluster: Wrap plain terracotta pots in different thicknesses of natural jute twine, cotton yarn, or raffia — glued in place — and group them together for a textural still-life.
  • Fabric swatch gallery: Frame squares of beautiful fabric — a kilim offcut, a piece of vintage sari fabric, a linen remnant — in simple wooden frames as a textile-textured alternative to traditional prints.
  • Dried botanical wall installation: Peg dried pampas grass, eucalyptus, or dried wildflowers directly to a wooden branch mounted on the wall. No frame needed — the organic shapes create living, three-dimensional texture.

Common Boho Texture Layering Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

After twelve years of doing this, I've seen the same mistakes come up again and again — and honestly, some of them I've made myself in the early days. The good news is they're all completely fixable once you know what to look for.

The mistake I always see most is people adding too much too fast. They buy eight cushions, three plants, two rugs, and a macramé wall hanging all in one week and then wonder why the room feels like a craft shop. Layering needs to be staged and edited, not assembled in one go.

Top Boho Texture Layering Mistakes and Fixes

  • Mistake: Too many pattern clashes. Fix: Stick to one strong pattern (a kilim rug, a printed cushion) and keep everything else tonal and textural.
  • Mistake: Everything at the same visual height. Fix: Use plants, floor lamps, and tall baskets to create a range of heights from floor to ceiling.
  • Mistake: Forgetting the floor. Fix: A layered rug situation — jute underneath, a smaller vintage rug on top — instantly creates a grounded, collected look.
  • Mistake: Buying all new pieces. Fix: Mix new with old, thrifted, or handmade. Boho looks most authentic when not everything matches.
  • Mistake: Neglecting the ceiling and upper wall space. Fix: Add hanging plants, ceiling-hung macramé, or a wall-mounted shelf at eye level and above to draw the eye upward and make the room feel layered in three dimensions.
  • Mistake: Treating texture as only about fabric. Fix: Include ceramic, wood, metal, glass, and plant materials — boho texture is about all materials, not just soft furnishings.
  • Mistake: Ignoring lighting as a texture tool. Fix: A rattan pendant shade or a terracotta lamp base adds texture and casts beautiful warm shadow patterns that visually deepen every other layer in the room.

The conversation around boho texture layering has shifted significantly in recent years — and interior designers agree that texture, not colour, is the true foundation of the look.

This approach tends to produce rooms that age well, feel genuinely personal, and work across changing trends because the tactile quality of natural materials doesn't date the way colour trends do. In practice, this means doing the materials work before you think about whether you want rust tones or indigo tones, statement pieces or quiet layers. Get the tactile mix right first, and the colour palette often resolves itself naturally from the materials you're drawn to.

Pro Tip: When you're struggling to make a boho room feel cohesive, go back to basics and audit your textures before your colours. Count how many genuinely different material types you have in the room. If the answer is fewer than four or five, that's usually where the flatness is coming from — not the colour palette.

The best way to layer textures in a boho style is to start with a neutral base, then build up in stages — rough naturals first, soft fabrics second, and decorative accents last — so every element earns its place without the room feeling cluttered or chaotic. These boho texture layering ideas work across every room and every budget, and I'm going to walk you through exactly how to do it.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in a room that felt genuinely warm and interesting — full of personality, all those gorgeous layers of fabric and natural material — and thought, "How on earth did they do that without it looking a mess?" I get asked this all the time, and it's exactly the kind of question I love answering, especially when it comes to wall art and the textural story it tells in a boho home.

Quick answer: Layer boho textures by starting with a neutral wall and floor, then adding rough naturals like jute and rattan, followed by soft layers such as woven throws and cushions, and finally decorative accents like macramé, plants, and wall art. Work room by room, keep your colour palette cohesive, and always step back to edit — less is almost always more than you think.

Boho style is one of the most misunderstood looks in home decor. It's not about piling everything you love onto every surface and hoping for the best. True boho layering is a considered process — a way of combining natural materials, handmade touches, global-inspired patterns, and unique wall art to create rooms that feel curated, not cluttered. When you add in the right unique home decor pieces, the whole thing clicks into place in a way that feels genuinely personal and lived-in.

Start with a Neutral Base for Boho Texture Layering

Before you add a single cushion or a woven wall hanging, you need a calm, neutral backdrop that lets your layers breathe. Think warm whites, soft creams, sandy beiges, and warm greiges — these give every subsequent layer somewhere to land without competing with it.

Your walls, your main flooring, and your largest furniture pieces should all sit in this neutral zone. If your sofa is already a bold colour or pattern, that's fine — just treat it as one of your mid layers rather than your base.

How to Build a Neutral Base

  • Walls: Choose warm white, linen, or soft clay. Avoid cool greys — they fight boho's earthy warmth.
  • Flooring: Natural wood, stone tile, or concrete are ideal. If you have carpet, a large flat-weave rug on top will anchor the base layer.
  • Large furniture: Stick to undyed linen, canvas, or cotton in oatmeal, cream, or warm taupe tones.
  • Ceiling: Keep it white or very pale. A warm-toned ceiling instantly lifts a room without adding visual noise.
  • Window treatments: Linen or cotton curtains in a natural, unbleached shade work perfectly as part of the base.

I once helped a client who'd painted her living room a lovely deep terracotta and then couldn't work out why all her boho layers looked too busy. The problem was there was no neutral breathing space — every single element was competing. We didn't repaint; instead, we pulled in much larger amounts of cream through a new rug and fresh linen throws, and it completely transformed the room.

Pro Tip: If you're renting and can't paint, use large-scale neutral textiles — a big cream linen throw draped over a sofa, sheer natural curtains, and a pale jute rug — to visually reset the base of the room without touching the walls.

Mix and Match Textures: Materials, Fabrics, and Finishes

Boho texture layering is all about contrast — rough against smooth, matte against sheen, natural against woven. The more genuinely different your materials feel to the touch, the more interesting the finished room looks to the eye.

The key rule I always come back to is this: never put two very similar textures next to each other. A jute rug next to a sisal basket works because the weave patterns are different enough. A jute rug next to a sisal cushion can look muddy and flat.

Boho Texture Material Pairings That Work

  • Jute + velvet: The ultimate boho contrast — rough and smooth in the same earthy colour family.
  • Rattan + linen: Rattan's geometric weave sits beautifully next to the soft drape of natural linen.
  • Ceramic + macramé: Hard, matte ceramics and soft, knotted cotton create real visual tension in a good way.
  • Sheepskin + woven cotton: Two soft textures that work because one is fluffy and dimensional, the other flat and structured.
  • Raw wood + silk-feel cushion covers: The roughness of undressed timber makes a lustrous fabric look even richer beside it.
  • Hammered brass + rough plaster wall: Metallic and matte create a striking but grounded combination.

Step-by-Step Boho Texture Layering Method for Walls and Decor

Layering textures isn't random — there's a real method to it, and once you understand it, you can apply it to any room. I think of it as working in four distinct passes, each one adding more specificity and personality than the last.

Don't try to do everything at once. Buy a piece, live with it for a few days, then add the next. Rushing is the single biggest reason boho rooms end up looking overwhelming rather than effortless.

The Four-Pass Method

  • Pass 1 — Neutral base: Walls, floor, and large furniture in calm neutrals (as covered above). This pass is mostly structural.
  • Pass 2 — Natural roughs: Add jute or sisal rugs, rattan furniture or accessories, wicker baskets, raw wooden shelves, terracotta pots. These ground the room with natural, earthy weight.
  • Pass 3 — Soft fabrics: Layer in throws, cushions, poufs, and curtains. Mix at least three different fabric textures — for example, a velvet cushion, a woven cotton throw, and a sheepskin.
  • Pass 4 — Decorative accents: This is where wall art, plants, candles, books, and small ceramics come in. These are the details that make the room feel personal and finished.

Here's what happened when I tried the four-pass method in my own flat's spare room: I kept buying Pass 4 items first — little pots, wall hangings, candles — and the room never came together. The moment I stripped it back and actually started with Pass 1, everything else found its place naturally. It felt like cheating, it was so much easier.

Pro Tip: After each pass, take a photo of the room on your phone. It's much easier to spot what's working and what's fighting for attention in a photo than it is standing in the space yourself.

Boho Wall Art as a Texture Layer: Prints, Tapestries, and Mixed Media

Wall art isn't just decoration in a boho room — it's a genuine texture layer in its own right. A woven tapestry adds the same kind of visual weight as a rug. A macramé wall hanging introduces knotted depth to a flat wall. Even a print in the right frame adds a matte-meets-glossy textural moment.

The mistake most people make is treating wall art as an afterthought — something to fill empty space once the room is "done." In boho layering, the wall is part of the texture story from the very beginning.

Types of Boho Wall Art That Add Texture

  • Woven tapestries: The original boho wall layer — handwoven pieces in natural fibres add warmth, pattern, and genuine three-dimensional texture.
  • Macramé wall hangings: Knotted cotton or jute with fringe; they cast soft shadows and add a sculptural quality to flat walls.
  • Botanical and earth-toned prints: Flat prints in natural palettes contribute colour and pattern as a texture layer without competing with tactile materials.
  • Mixed-media art: Pieces that incorporate fabrics, beads, or natural materials within the artwork itself add real physical depth.
  • Dried botanical wreaths and wall installations: Pampas grass, dried flowers, and hanging eucalyptus bring organic, three-dimensional texture directly to the wall surface.
  • Gallery walls with varied frame finishes: Mixing raw wood, rattan-wrapped, and thin black frames creates textural variety even before you look at what's inside the frames.

Real Example: A client of mine had a huge blank wall in her living room and wanted a gallery wall but had almost no budget. We mixed a single large botanical print she'd ordered online with two macramé wall hangings from a craft market and a small round rattan mirror. The combination of flat print, knotted textile, and reflective surface created three distinct texture moments — and the whole wall cost less than she expected.

Room-by-Room Boho Texture Layering Guides

Different rooms have different needs when it comes to texture layering, and what works in a bedroom can feel completely wrong in an entryway. Here's how I approach each key space so the boho layering feels right for the room's function, not just its look.

Think about how each room is used and what feeling you want it to create. The bedroom should feel enveloping and restful. The living room should feel sociable and interesting. The entryway should feel welcoming and just a little surprising.

Bedroom Texture Layering

  • Start with natural linen or cotton bedding in cream or warm white — this is your base.
  • Layer a chunky knit or woven throw across the foot of the bed for tactile depth.
  • Add cushions in at least three different textures: velvet, woven cotton, and a bead-embroidered or embroidered cushion.
  • Hang a large macramé or woven textile above the bed instead of a headboard, or above a traditional headboard for extra texture height.
  • Use rattan or wicker beside tables, a sheepskin on the floor beside the bed, and trailing plants to bring the layering all the way to floor level.

Living Room Texture Layering

  • Ground the room with a large jute or flat-weave rug — size up; too-small rugs make layering look disjointed.
  • Layer a second, smaller patterned rug on top for a collected, well-travelled feel.
  • Mix sofa cushions across at least four textures: woven, velvet, embroidered, and tasselled.
  • Bring rattan, wicker, or woven baskets in as storage that also works as decor.
  • Use plants at different heights — a tall floor plant, a mid-height shelf plant, and trailing plants at high level to soften vertical space.

Entryway Texture Layering

  • A natural coir or jute doormat with a printed pattern introduces texture from the first step inside.
  • Add a small rattan console or wooden bench as the structural anchor.
  • Hang a macramé wall piece, a small mirror with a rattan or wooden frame, or a cluster of dried botanical wreaths on the wall.
  • A tall wicker basket for umbrellas or throws adds practical texture at floor level.
  • Layer a ceramic pot with a plant — trailing or compact — to soften the corner and bring life to the space immediately.

Pro Tip: In small entryways, resist the temptation to layer too many pieces. One great textile moment — a macramé hanging or a woven mirror frame — and two or three natural material accents is usually all you need. The goal is "interesting first impression," not a museum of objects.

Specific Product and Material Recommendations with Styling Tips

People ask me constantly where to start when it comes to actually buying for a boho textured room. My honest answer is always: start with the biggest textural impact per pound spent. That usually means rugs, throws, and wall hangings before anything else.

Here's a breakdown of the specific materials I reach for most often, and how I actually use them in a styled room rather than just placing them straight out of the bag.

Colour Palette Guidance for Cohesive Boho Layered Looks

The single biggest thing that separates a boho room that looks professionally styled from one that just looks chaotic is a disciplined colour palette. Boho doesn't mean every colour at once — it means deep, earthy tones used with intention.

I always work to what I call a 3-1-1 palette: three neutral tones, one warm earth accent, and one deeper or contrasting pop. Everything in the room maps back to these five tones, no matter how varied the textures are.

Boho Colour Palette Rules

  • Neutrals (the majority): Warm white, cream, sand, linen, oatmeal — these should make up at least 60% of the room's visual colour.
  • Earth accent (the personality): Rust, terracotta, warm ochre, amber, or burnt sienna — introduce this through cushions, pots, throws, and wall art.
  • Deep pop (the drama): Deep teal, indigo, forest green, or aubergine — just one or two pieces in this tone to stop the room feeling too one-note.
  • Metallic (the finish): Warm brass or antique gold accents read as neutral in a boho palette but add a subtle luminosity that lifts natural materials.
  • What to avoid: Cool greys, bright white, neon tones, and pastel pinks — all of these fight the warm, earthy heart of boho style.
Real Example: A client came to me having bought a beautiful rust-coloured sofa and then couldn't work out why the room still felt cold and unresolved. The issue was that everything else was cool grey — walls, rug, cushions. We warmed up the walls with a sand-toned paint, swapped the rug for a jute one, and added cream and deep forest green accents. Same sofa, completely transformed room. The colour palette was the whole answer.

DIY Boho Texture Layering Projects You Can Try at Home

One of the things I genuinely love about boho style is that it rewards making things yourself. Handmade, imperfect, slightly organic — these qualities are the whole point. A shop-bought version of a macramé wall hanging will always look a little too perfect compared to the one you made yourself, and that imperfection is exactly what gives it its charm.

You don't need to be crafty in a serious way. These projects are all accessible, genuinely achievable in an afternoon, and add real textural interest to a room.

DIY Projects with Big Textural Impact

  • Basic macramé wall hanging: A wooden dowel and natural cotton cord are all you need. Square knots and half-hitch knots are beginner-level and create beautiful results. Fringe the ends for extra texture.
  • Dip-dyed fabric wall panel: Take a length of unbleached cotton canvas and dip the bottom third into fabric dye in a rust or indigo tone. Hang from a dowel when dry — it reads as abstract art with genuine textile texture.
  • Woven branch mobile: Collect interesting branches from outdoors, tie them together with jute twine, and hang small bundles of dried flowers, feathers, or beads from the lower branches. This is a genuine three-dimensional texture layer for the ceiling or a corner.
  • Yarn-wrapped pot cluster: Wrap plain terracotta pots in different thicknesses of natural jute twine, cotton yarn, or raffia — glued in place — and group them together for a textural still-life.
  • Fabric swatch gallery: Frame squares of beautiful fabric — a kilim offcut, a piece of vintage sari fabric, a linen remnant — in simple wooden frames as a textile-textured alternative to traditional prints.
  • Dried botanical wall installation: Peg dried pampas grass, eucalyptus, or dried wildflowers directly to a wooden branch mounted on the wall. No frame needed — the organic shapes create living, three-dimensional texture.

Pro Tip: The best DIY boho texture pieces tend to be the ones you make slightly too large. Scale up — a macramé hanging that feels almost too wide for the wall, or a branch mobile that reaches almost to the ceiling — makes a much stronger textural statement than a modest, safe-sized piece.

How to Layer Textures on a Budget Using Thrifted and Affordable Pieces

Here's a truth nobody in home decor talks about enough: boho style is one of the most budget-friendly aesthetics going, because it actively celebrates things that are old, found, handmade, or imperfect. You do not need to spend a lot of money to do this well.

Some of the best boho textured rooms I've worked on have been built almost entirely from charity shops, car boot sales, and market stalls. The key is knowing what to look for and what to skip.

Budget Boho Texture Layering Tips

  • Charity shops and car boot sales: Look for woven throws, kilim cushion covers, rattan trays, wooden frames, and ceramic pots. These are the exact items that get donated most often and cost a fraction of new.
  • Natural materials from outdoors: Branches, smooth pebbles, dried seed heads, and pinecones are free texture layers that look genuinely beautiful in a boho styled room.
  • Supermarket buys: Many supermarkets stock affordable terracotta pots, wicker baskets, and linen-look cushion covers — keep an eye on seasonal home sections.
  • Fabric remnants: Visit fabric shops and ask for offcuts — kilim remnants, cotton canvas, and linen remnants can all become cushion covers, wall hangings, or framed textile art.
  • Facebook Marketplace and Gumtree: Rattan furniture, wooden shelves, and vintage rugs come up regularly and can often be collected for very little.
  • Repurpose what you have: An old wooden crate becomes a side table. A vintage scarf becomes a throw or a wall hanging. A jam jar becomes a candle holder or a small vase.
Pro Tip: Don't try to buy everything at once even if your budget allows it. The rooms that look most authentically boho are the ones that have been built up slowly over time — a piece here, something found there. Give yourself permission to build gradually and the result will always look more genuine than a room bought in one afternoon.

Common Boho Texture Layering Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

After twelve years of doing this, I've seen the same mistakes come up again and again — and honestly, some of them I've made myself in the early days. The good news is they're all completely fixable once you know what to look for.

The mistake I always see most is people adding too much too fast. They buy eight cushions, three plants, two rugs, and a macramé wall hanging all in one week and then wonder why the room feels like a craft shop. Layering needs to be staged and edited, not assembled in one go.

Top Boho Texture Layering Mistakes and Fixes

  • Mistake: Too many pattern clashes. Fix: Stick to one strong pattern (a kilim rug, a printed cushion) and keep everything else tonal and textural.
  • Mistake: Everything at the same visual height. Fix: Use plants, floor lamps, and tall baskets to create a range of heights from floor to ceiling.
  • Mistake: Forgetting the floor. Fix: A layered rug situation — jute underneath, a smaller vintage rug on top — instantly creates a grounded, collected look.
  • Mistake: Buying all new pieces. Fix: Mix new with old, thrifted, or handmade. Boho looks most authentic when not everything matches.
  • Mistake: Neglecting the ceiling and upper wall space. Fix: Add hanging plants, ceiling-hung macramé, or a wall-mounted shelf at eye level and above to draw the eye upward and make the room feel layered in three dimensions.
  • Mistake: Treating texture as only about fabric. Fix: Include ceramic, wood, metal, glass, and plant materials — boho texture is about all materials, not just soft furnishings.
  • Mistake: Ignoring lighting as a texture tool. Fix: A rattan pendant shade or a terracotta lamp base adds texture and casts beautiful warm shadow patterns that visually deepen every other layer in the room.

Real Example: The most common client situation I see is someone who has bought everything in the "right" boho style but the room still feels flat. Nine times out of ten the problem is lighting — they have harsh overhead ceiling lights and nothing else. Swapping in a warm-toned rattan pendant and adding a couple of table lamps with warm-white bulbs transforms the texture layering completely, because warm light makes every woven, carved, and natural material cast shadow and depth.

Boho isn't one thing — it's a family of related aesthetics, and knowing which direction suits you makes buying decisions so much cleaner.

More About Boho Texture Layering: What the Experts Say

The conversation around boho texture layering has shifted significantly in recent years — and interior designers agree that texture, not colour, is the true foundation of the look.

More and more design experts are recommending that you build a boho bedroom — and any boho room — around texture as the primary design decision rather than leading with colour, pattern, or a specific aesthetic mood board. This approach tends to produce rooms that age well, feel genuinely personal, and work across changing trends because the tactile quality of natural materials doesn't date the way colour trends do. You can read more about this approach in How to Build a Boho Bedroom Around Texture Instead of Color - StyleGuru, which makes a compelling case for texture-first thinking across the whole home.

In practice, this means doing the materials work before you think about whether you want rust tones or indigo tones, statement pieces or quiet layers. Get the tactile mix right first, and the colour palette often resolves itself naturally from the materials you're drawn to.

Pro Tip: When you're struggling to make a boho room feel cohesive, go back to basics and audit your textures before your colours. Count how many genuinely different material types you have in the room. If the answer is fewer than four or five, that's usually where the flatness is coming from — not the colour palette.

Ready to Start Your Own Boho Texture Layering?

Boho texture layering is genuinely one of the most enjoyable things you can do in a home. There are no rigid rules, mistakes are usually fixable, and the process of building a room up layer by layer — watching it come to life over time — is deeply satisfying in a way that a one-weekend room refresh never quite is.

Start small. Pick one corner, one wall, or just your bed. Get the neutral base right, add two or three genuinely different natural textures, and see how it feels before you add anything else. You'll quickly develop a sense for what the space needs next, and that instinct is really what boho texture layering is all about.

The rooms I'm most proud of — mine and my clients' — all started with just one great piece and grew from there. They weren't planned on a mood board; they were built through curiosity and patience.

So tell me — which room in your home are you thinking about tackling first, and what's the one texture you're most excited to bring into it?

accent walls in kitchens: practical or t.bodyHtml:
Kitchen accent wall ideas are absolutely worth considering — they can transform a hardworking, functional space into something that actually feels like part of your home rather than an afterthought. Whether you're after a bold statement or a subtle backdrop, an accent wall in the kitchen is both practical and on-trend when done right.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever walked into your kitchen, looked around, and thought — something's missing, but I can't quite put my finger on it? That feeling is more common than you'd think, and more often than not, the answer is somewhere on your walls. A well-chosen piece of wall art or a thoughtfully designed feature wall can completely shift the energy of a room you spend hours in every day.

Quick answer: Kitchen accent walls are both practical and stylish — they add personality without a full renovation, and with the right material (tile, paint, shiplap, stone or wallpaper) they're surprisingly durable in a kitchen setting. The key is choosing the right wall, the right material for the job, and styling around it thoughtfully.

An accent wall, simply put, is one wall in a room that's treated differently from the rest — through colour, texture, pattern or material — to create a focal point. In kitchens, this idea has properly come into its own because it gives you a way to inject personality into a room that's often dominated by cabinetry and appliances. Pairing a well-executed feature wall with unique wall art and carefully chosen unique home decor can pull the whole look together beautifully.

Types of Kitchen Accent Walls: Paint, Tile, Shiplap, Wallpaper, and Stone

The material you choose for your kitchen accent wall sets the entire tone — not just visually, but practically too. Each option has its own personality, its own maintenance requirements, and its own sweet spot in terms of where it works best in a kitchen.

Paint is the most approachable starting point. A single wall in a deep forest green, warm terracotta or inky navy can completely reframe a kitchen without any specialist skills. The trick is using a satin or semi-gloss finish in a kitchen so the surface is wipeable — flat paints look gorgeous in living rooms but they're a nightmare near a hob.

Your Main Material Options at a Glance

  • Paint: Most affordable and reversible — use satin or semi-gloss finish for kitchen use. Ideal for any wall in the room.
  • Tile: Incredibly durable and easy to clean — perfect for behind a hob or sink. Can be bold and decorative or understated and textural.
  • Shiplap / timber cladding: Adds warmth and texture beautifully — works well on non-cooking walls. Seal it properly to protect from steam and grease.
  • Wallpaper: Modern kitchen wallpapers are more robust than you'd think — choose vinyl-coated or washable options. Avoid directly behind the hob.
  • Stone / stone-effect panels: Luxurious and dramatic — natural stone, brick slips or engineered panels all work. Heavier to install but stunning results.
  • Brick slips: Raw, industrial feel — real or faux brick slips are a great budget-friendlier alternative to full stonework.

I once helped a client in a Victorian terrace who desperately wanted exposed brick in her kitchen but had solid plastered walls. We used brick slips on just the chimney breast alcove wall — the effect was completely convincing and the cost was a fraction of what she'd feared.

Pro Tip: Whatever material you choose, always check it's rated for kitchen use — specifically that it can handle humidity, grease splashes and temperature changes. What works in a dining room won't always survive near a hob.

How to Choose the Right Wall for Your Kitchen Accent

This is where a lot of people trip up — they pick a material or colour they love and then slap it on whichever wall is easiest, rather than thinking about which wall will actually do the most work. Choosing the right wall first makes everything else fall into place.

The best accent wall is usually the one your eye naturally falls on when you enter the room. In most kitchens that's either the wall behind the hob, the wall at the end of a galley, or the wall opposite the main window. Think about sightlines — what do you see from the living area if it's open-plan? What do you see from the kitchen doorway?

Questions to Ask Before You Decide

  • Which wall do you naturally look at most when you're in the kitchen?
  • Is the wall near a heat or moisture source? (This affects your material choices.)
  • Does the wall have windows, doors, or sockets that will interrupt the design?
  • What's on the other side of this wall in an open-plan space — will the accent wall read well from the living or dining area too?
  • Is it a solid wall, or is there pipework or boxing that might complicate installation?
  • How much natural light does the wall receive — darker materials need good light to avoid feeling oppressive.
Real Example: A client of mine had her heart set on the wall beside the back door as her accent wall. When we looked at it together, we realised it was interrupted by a boiler cupboard, a light switch, a plug socket, and a small window — essentially four features breaking up the space. We switched focus to the wall behind her cooker instead, which was uninterrupted and visible from the dining table. It was a much stronger choice.

How to Style and Decorate Around a Kitchen Accent Wall

Getting the accent wall itself right is only half the job. What you put in front of it and around it is what turns a nice wall into a properly styled kitchen. The accent wall should feel like the backdrop to a curated scene, not a standalone feature with nothing supporting it.

The mistake I always see is people creating a beautiful feature wall and then leaving the surfaces in front of it completely empty or cluttered with random bits and pieces. The wall needs companions — open shelving with considered styling, a collection of ceramics, some pendant lighting, or a piece of art that echoes the wall's colour.

Styling Tips for Around Your Accent Wall

  • Open shelving: Mount open shelves directly on the accent wall — styled with a mix of ceramics, plants, glassware and a couple of cookbooks. This integrates the wall into the room's functionality.
  • Lighting: Wall-mounted sconces or under-cabinet lighting can draw attention to the accent wall beautifully. Pendant lights hanging in front of it add depth.
  • Plants: A trailing plant on a shelf or a wall-mounted planter softens bold colours and adds life to the wall.
  • Mirrors: A simple mirror on or near an accent wall adds light and visual interest without competing with the wall's colour or texture.
  • Worktop accessories: Keep the surface directly in front of your accent wall considered — a wooden chopping board, a stone mortar and pestle, a small plant. Not empty, not chaotic.
  • Repeat the colour: Echo the accent wall colour in small accessories throughout the kitchen — a tea towel, a ceramic pot, a vase — to make the whole room feel intentional.
Pro Tip: Don't overload the accent wall itself with too many things. Its job is to be a backdrop — one or two carefully chosen elements mounted on it is usually better than five competing pieces.

Small Kitchen Accent Wall — Dos and Don'ts

  • Do choose the end wall of a galley or the wall opposite the doorway for maximum visual depth.
  • Do consider warm tones — terracotta, mustard, warm green — which feel cosy rather than closing.
  • Do keep the other walls pale and light to avoid the space feeling smaller.
  • Do use a half-wall treatment — paint or tile the lower half and keep the top pale — to give visual breathing room.
  • Don't use a very large, busy pattern in a tiny kitchen — it can feel overwhelming rather than characterful.
  • Don't use the accent wall to hide badly proportioned cabinetry — the wall will draw more attention to the problem, not less.
  • Don't forget lighting — a small kitchen accent wall needs decent light to sing, not a dim overhead bulb.
Real Example: I worked with a client in a London flat with a genuinely tiny galley kitchen — maybe two metres wide and four metres long. She painted the end wall in a deep warm green while keeping everything else white, added a single wooden shelf with a few ceramics, and the whole kitchen felt like it had a proper identity rather than just being a functional corridor. Making an Accent Wall Work Across an Open-Plan Space

  • Anchor the kitchen zone: An accent wall is a brilliant way to visually define the kitchen within an open-plan space — it signals "this is the kitchen" without needing physical walls.
  • Repeat the colour in the living or dining area: Echo the accent wall colour in cushions, a rug, or a throw on the sofa — this creates visual flow rather than a jarring boundary.
  • Mind the sightlines: Stand in the sofa and look at the kitchen — that's your guest's view. The accent wall should look intentional and considered from that angle.
  • Keep the transition wall neutral: The wall that bridges the kitchen and living zone should stay pale or neutral so it doesn't compete with the accent wall.
  • Consider material cohesion: If you have a timber floor running through both spaces, a timber shiplap accent wall in the kitchen will feel harmonious rather than disconnected.
  • Use lighting to unify: Consistent pendant styles across the kitchen island and dining table help the open-plan space feel curated rather than accidental.
Pro Tip: In an open-plan space, the accent wall works best when it's on the kitchen-side of the room rather than on a shared wall between zones. It defines the kitchen without boxing it in.

Wall Art Choices That Work Beautifully in Kitchens

  • Botanical prints: A timeless choice — herb illustrations, fruit studies, and leaf prints all feel at home in a kitchen and work across a wide range of accent wall colours.
  • Abstract prints: A simple abstract in tones that echo your accent wall colour ties the look together without being too literal.
  • Food and drink illustrations: Think wine bottles, coffee cups, or market produce — these feel genuinely at home in a kitchen and can be witty and personal.
  • Typography prints: A favourite recipe or a simple kitchen-related quote can add personality without being kitsch if kept in the right style.
  • Photography prints: Black and white photography looks striking against a bold colour, and travel or nature photography can personalise the space beautifully.
  • Scale matters: In a kitchen, medium-scale prints tend to work better than very large canvases — the cabinetry and shelving create a lot of visual competition, so a focused, well-placed print lands better than an oversized piece.

My rule of thumb: if the accent wall is very bold in colour or pattern, choose simpler, quieter art. If the accent wall is more textural or subtle — shiplap or stone, for example — you can afford more character in the artwork.

Renter-Friendly Accent Wall Options

  • Peel-and-stick wallpaper: Comes in hundreds of patterns and colours — applies cleanly to smooth walls and removes without damage. Always test in a small section first.

  • Fabric wall hangings: A large macramé or woven textile hung on a wooden dowel creates a soft, textural feature without touching the wall finish at all.
  • Picture ledges: Command strip-mounted picture ledges or rails mean you can display a collection of prints and artwork without drilling — and take them all with you when you leave.

Step-by-Step Planning Guide Before Starting a Kitchen Accent Wall

The biggest mistake people make with kitchen accent walls isn't choosing the wrong colour — it's skipping the planning stage altogether and discovering halfway through that there's a problem they didn't anticipate. A little upfront work saves a lot of undoing.

I always take clients through a proper planning process before anything gets purchased or ordered. It sounds boring but it prevents the kind of expensive mistakes that are genuinely common — and genuinely avoidable.

Your Pre-Start Planning Checklist

  • Step 1 — Choose your wall: Decide which wall based on sightlines, natural light, and how it's used (is it near the hob? Near a sink? On an exterior wall that might be damp?).
  • Step 2 — Check the wall's condition: Is the plaster sound? Any damp? Any pipes or cables behind it you need to be aware of? Never tile or panel over a damp wall.
  • Step 3 — Measure accurately: Measure the wall's width and height and account for any windows, doors, or sockets. Calculate the area in square metres for ordering materials.
  • Step 4 — Order samples: Never order materials at full quantity without seeing samples first. For paint, get a large tester pot and paint a proper swatch. For tiles or wallpaper, order a sample panel.
  • Step 5 — Live with your sample: Leave your sample up for at least a week before committing. Look at it in the morning light, the evening light, under artificial light. Colours behave differently at different times of day.
  • Step 6 — Plan your styling before you start: Decide what shelves, lighting, art or accessories will go around the wall before you order the wall material — it changes what you choose and how much you spend.
  • Step 7 — Set a realistic budget: Include not just the material and installation, but any prep work (plaster repair, primer), accessories, and contingency for over-ordering.
  • Step 8 — Professional or DIY? Be honest with yourself. Tiling and stone installation usually benefits from professional hands. Paint and removable wallpaper are genuinely DIY-friendly.
Pro Tip: Always order 10-15% more material than your measurements suggest — for tiles in particular, you'll need spares for cuts, breakages and future repairs. Running out of a discontinued tile pattern halfway through is a very unpleasant situation to be in.

- Lighting: Bridge-style or vintage-inspired polished nickel and chrome fixtures, botanical or leaf-sculpted chandelier forms in matte white or whitewashed metal, ambient natural daylight flooding from large-pane windows, soft diffused fill with no harsh shadows
- Plants: Small potted herbs or single-stem botanicals in simple vessels, kept restrained and naturalistic rather than lush; dried grasses or wheat stems as a secondary option
- Wall decor: Vertical shiplap or beadboard panelling as the primary wall texture, simple framed ledges or plate rails where needed, sconces in brushed nickel or matte white, NO framed prints as default (the shop's wall art is added separately as product photos)
- Ceramics/objects: Handmade-looking stoneware in cream, warm white, and stripe-banded blue and white, glass hurricane vessels, simple silver or pewter trays, cookbooks stacked as functional objects; vary the pieces to suit each room
- Textiles: Ticking-stripe cotton in soft blue and white, linen in natural undyed tones, loose-weave cotton throws, no heavy pattern; textures should feel washed, relaxed, and slightly rumpled rather than pressed
- Mood: Bright, airy, quietly nostalgic
- White balance: Neutral-to-cool white balance, preserving clean crisp whites with no yellow or warm cast while allowing natural daylight to feel luminous
- No: High-gloss or shiny lacquered furniture, industrial black metal frames, overly polished surfaces, maximalist colour, dark moody walls, mid-century silhouettes, bohemian or macrame elements, plastic or synthetic-looking materials
